newsitem.title: USA: Disability rate among U.S. elderly declines.
newsitem.headline: Disability rate among U.S. elderly declines.

text.p: Chronic disability among older Americans has dropped steadily since the early 1980s, a finding that may shape the debate over Medicare and other government health programs, Duke University researchers said on Monday.

It is well-known that Americans are living longer, but the study appearing on Tuesday in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences suggests people do not spend all their senior years disabled. Rather, more people remain reasonably fit and independent until late in life.

"When we speak of the 'old-old,' we now usually mean people who are 85 or older. Functionally speaking, a 65-year-old today is much younger than a 65-year-old" was a generation ago, Duke demographer Kenneth Manton said in a telephone interview from the Durham, N.C. campus.

The Duke demographers said the chronic disability rate for people 65 and older dropped by 15 percent from 1982 to 1994. The decline was most pronounced in the final five years studied, and among the older and most disabled populations.
By definition, the chronically disabled are people in a long-term care setting or people who cannot take care of themselves on a daily basis for at least three months.

There were 7.1 million chronically disabled people in the nation in 1994, many on Medicare or Medicaid. The demographers wrote that had the disability rate remained steady, there would have been 1.2 million more older disabled people.

Manton said the findings did not have much bearing on the short-term financing problems of Medicare, which covers everyone over age 65, and Medicaid, which covers many elderly people in nursing homes. Medicare's hospital trust fund is heading for bankruptcy shortly after the turn of the century.
But he said the findings would have implications for longer-term reforms of Medicare to cope with the surge of baby boomers who start retiring in about 2012.
"There are going to have to be policy fixes in the short term. But there's a different dynamic for the babyboomers," he said.

The team wrote in the journal, "If declines in chronic disability continue, the magnitude of changes required in the Medicare (and Medicaid) benefits might be reduced," Manton and his colleagues wrote in the journal.

Commenting on the Duke study in a speech on Medicare, Sen. Edward Kennedy, a Massachusetts Democrat, said a disabled senior citizen typically costs Medicare four to seven times as much as a non-disabled beneficiary.
He said instead of cutting Medicare benefits, the emphasis should be on spending money to keep people healthy, partly by better health education and preventive medicine.
"Senior citizens will enjoy longer lives. The overall savings from their better health will outweigh the additional cost of providing health care for a larger number of the elderly," Kennedy said.
